mcqs.question: Which property of XOR is what allows you to XOR an entire array together in a single pass, in any order, and still get the correct paired-cancellation result?
options: a ^ 0 = a alone
That XOR always returns a non-negative result
That XOR is a linear operation over real numbers
That XOR is commutative and associative, so grouping and order don't affect the result
mcqs.explanation: Commutativity and associativity mean a ^ b ^ c is the same regardless of order or grouping, which is exactly what guarantees a single left-to-right pass finds every pair and cancels it no matter where in the array the pair's two elements sit. a ^ 0 = a explains why the lone survivor passes through untouched, but it doesn't explain why order-independence holds, and XOR isn't a real-number linear operation.

mcqs.question: Why does the plain XOR-fold solution to Single Number I use O(1) extra space instead of the O(n) a hash-map counting approach needs?
options: Because it only keeps a single running accumulator variable, never storing per-element counts
Because XOR is faster than addition, which reduces memory usage
Because the input array itself is modified in place to save space
Because it only works on arrays smaller than a fixed size
mcqs.explanation: The XOR fold needs exactly one integer to accumulate the running XOR — nothing per-element is ever stored, unlike a hash map that tracks a count for every distinct value seen. Speed of XOR versus addition is irrelevant to space complexity, the array isn't mutated, and there's no size restriction on correctness.

mcqs.question: Why does a plain XOR fold fail to solve Single Number II, where every element appears three times except one?
options: XOR-ing three copies of the same value together returns that value itself, not zero, so it pollutes the result instead of cancelling
XOR can only combine an even number of values correctly
The array needs to be sorted first for XOR to work with triples
XOR overflows once a value appears more than twice
mcqs.explanation: Two of the three copies cancel to zero, but the third copy XORs against that zero and survives unchanged — so a tripled value contaminates the fold instead of vanishing the way a doubled value does. XOR doesn't require sorting or an even count in general, and it doesn't overflow; the failure is specific to how three identical copies interact under XOR's cancellation rule.

mcqs.question: In Single Number III, after XOR-folding the whole array to get `combined = unique1 ^ unique2`, why do you split the array using a bit where `combined` has a 1?
options: Because that bit is guaranteed to be 0 in both unique1 and unique2
Because that bit must differ between unique1 and unique2, guaranteeing the two of them land in different groups while every paired value's two copies stay together
Because it's an arbitrary choice with no effect on correctness
Because that bit identifies which value is larger
mcqs.explanation: A 1 in combined at that position means unique1 and unique2 disagree there, so splitting on it always separates them into different groups, while any paired value's identical copies agree on every bit and always land together in the same group, cancelling within it. It isn't arbitrary, doesn't imply either value has a 0 there, and has nothing to do with numeric ordering.

mcqs.question: For finding a missing number in the range 0..n, what advantage does the XOR-based approach have over the sum-based formula n*(n+1)/2 minus the actual sum?
options: It's asymptotically faster, running in O(log n) instead of O(n)
It works even when the array contains duplicate values
It never overflows in fixed-width integer types, since XOR never produces a value wider than its inputs
It doesn't require iterating over the full array
mcqs.explanation: The sum formula can overflow a fixed-width integer type for large n before the subtraction ever happens, while XOR-ing bounded-width values can never exceed the width of the inputs, so it sidesteps that failure mode entirely. Both approaches are O(n) and require a full pass, and the missing-number problem's premise already assumes distinct values, not duplicates.

mcqs.question: Before reaching for a Single Number-style XOR fold on a new problem, what should you confirm first?
options: That the array is sorted in ascending order
The exact, guaranteed duplication pattern — for example, that every value truly appears exactly twice except one
That the array has an even total length
That every value is non-negative
mcqs.explanation: XOR folding is correct only for a precise, known duplication shape; if the actual pattern differs from what you assumed — say some values appear four times, or the pattern is mixed across the array — a plain fold or modulo trick can silently return a wrong answer. Sort order, total array length parity, and sign of the values aren't what makes the trick valid or invalid.
